"Each customer's most recent order" (use ROW_NUMBER to get exactly one row per customer even with ties):

SQL
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders
)
SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY customer_id;
Result
customer_id order_id order_date
C0001 IN-2025-02263 2025-04-09
C0002 IN-2025-02871 2025-10-21
C0003 IN-2025-02642 2025-08-18
C0004 IN-2025-02344 2025-05-10
C0005 IN-2025-02982 2025-11-12
C0006 IN-2025-02960 2025-11-08
785 rows × 3 columns (first 6 shown)

Nth highest per group

"Second-highest paid employee in each department" (a top interview question):

SQL
WITH r AS (
    SELECT department, emp_id, monthly_income,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY monthly_income DESC) AS rnk
    FROM employees
)
SELECT department, emp_id, monthly_income
FROM r
WHERE rnk = 2
ORDER BY department;
Result
department emp_id monthly_income
Finance E00145 185500
HR E00450 175750
IT E01473 194500
Operations E00378 184167
R&D E00580 188083
Sales E01218 184833
6 rows × 3 columns

Use DENSE_RANK for "Nth highest value" (ties share a position, no gaps) and ROW_NUMBER for "Nth row".

Removing duplicates with ROW_NUMBER

SQL
WITH d AS (
    SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id, order_date, product_id ORDER BY item_id) AS rn
    FROM order_items_raw
)
DELETE FROM d WHERE rn > 1;            -- SQL Server lets you DELETE through a CTE

Rows with the same business key get numbers 1, 2, 3…; keeping rn = 1 keeps one copy. Always check with a SELECT … WHERE rn > 1 first.

Let's count how many lines in our data repeat the same product in the same order (what a de-duplication would touch):

SQL
WITH d AS (
    SELECT order_id, product_id,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id, product_id ORDER BY row_id) AS rn
    FROM superstore
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS repeated_lines FROM d WHERE rn > 1;
Result
repeated_lines
70
1 rows × 1 columns

(These are legitimate repeat lines, not errors; the point is the pattern.)

NTILE: buckets and percentiles

SQL
WITH cust AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(sales) AS sales FROM superstore GROUP BY customer_id
), q AS (
    SELECT customer_id, sales, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY sales DESC) AS quartile FROM cust
)
SELECT quartile,
       COUNT(*)               AS customers,
       ROUND(SUM(sales), 0)   AS sales,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(sales) / SUM(SUM(sales)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_total_sales
FROM q
GROUP BY quartile
ORDER BY quartile;
Result
quartile customers sales pct_of_total_sales
1 197 111,100,409 55.2
2 196 54,386,341 27.0
3 196 28,080,117 13.9
4 196 7,846,704 3.9
4 rows × 4 columns

Quartile 1 (the top 25% of customers) generates a disproportionate share of sales: the Pareto principle from the Excel charts lesson, now computed in SQL. NTILE is also how RFM scoring is done (ML track).

Aggregate window functions

Any aggregate (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX) becomes a window function with OVER. Without ORDER BY in the window, it uses the whole partition: perfect for totals, shares and comparisons with the group average.

SQL
SELECT department, emp_id, monthly_income,
       ROUND(AVG(monthly_income) OVER (PARTITION BY department), 0)           AS dept_avg,
       monthly_income - ROUND(AVG(monthly_income) OVER (PARTITION BY department), 0) AS vs_dept_avg,
       COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY department)                                AS dept_headcount,
       MAX(monthly_income) OVER (PARTITION BY department)                     AS dept_max
FROM employees
ORDER BY department, monthly_income DESC;
Result
department emp_id monthly_income dept_avg vs_dept_avg dept_headcount dept_max
Finance E00519 209833 83,681 126,152 154 209833
Finance E00145 185500 83,681 101,819 154 209833
Finance E00336 174417 83,681 90,736 154 209833
Finance E00201 169500 83,681 85,819 154 209833
Finance E01172 168167 83,681 84,486 154 209833
Finance E01151 155167 83,681 71,486 154 209833
Finance E00759 152083 83,681 68,402 154 209833
Finance E01004 144667 83,681 60,986 154 209833
1,500 rows × 7 columns (first 8 shown)

This replaces the correlated subquery from Lesson 10 ("earns more than the department average") with one pass over the data.

GROUP BY vs window functions

GROUP BY Window function
Rows returned One per group Same as input
Detail columns Only grouped columns All columns
Use for Summary reports Rankings, running totals, shares, comparisons with group values
Filter the result HAVING Wrap in CTE/subquery and WHERE
Can combine Yes: group first, then window over the groups

Summary

Key takeaways
  • OFFSET n ROWS FETCH NEXT m ROWS ONLY (with ORDER BY) paginates; it can skip rows, unlike TOP.
  • A window function adds a calculation over a set of related rows to each row, without collapsing them. OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …) defines the window.
  • ROW_NUMBER (unique), RANK (ties, gaps), DENSE_RANK (ties, no gaps), NTILE(n) (equal buckets).
  • To filter on a window result, compute it in a CTE or derived table, then use WHERE.
  • Top-N per group and Nth highest per group: DENSE_RANK/ROW_NUMBER partitioned by group; de-duplicate with ROW_NUMBER … WHERE rn > 1.
  • Aggregate windows (SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY …)) show totals, shares and group averages beside each row.
Quick quiz6 questions · tap an answer to check it

1. Scores 100, 90, 90, 80. What does DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) return?

Answer: C. DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same rank and continues without gaps.

2. Why can't you write WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1?

Answer: B. Logical processing order: WHERE runs before SELECT, where windows are computed.

3. What is the difference between PARTITION BY and GROUP BY?

Answer: B. Partitions restart the calculation for each group without reducing the number of rows.

4. Which returns the 3rd highest distinct salary overall?

Answer: A. DENSE_RANK counts distinct values; ROW_NUMBER would count rows even if values repeat.

5. SUM(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY region) returns:

Answer: B. Without ORDER BY in the window, it sums the whole partition.

6. To fetch rows 21–30 of a sorted result you write:

Answer: B. Skip 20, take 10.
ExerciseWindow practice

(1) For each customer segment, rank customers by total sales and show the top 3. (2) For each order line, show its sales as a percentage of its order's total. (3) For each department, list employees whose income is within the top 5% of their department (use NTILE(20)). (4) Show products whose total sales rank in the top 10% of their category.

Show solution
SQL
-- (1)
WITH t AS (SELECT c.segment, c.customer_name, SUM(oi.sales) AS sales
           FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
           GROUP BY c.segment, c.customer_id, c.customer_name),
     r AS (SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY segment ORDER BY sales DESC) AS rnk FROM t)
SELECT * FROM r WHERE rnk <= 3 ORDER BY segment, rnk;
-- (2)
SELECT item_id, order_id, sales, ROUND(100.0 * sales / SUM(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY order_id), 1) AS pct_of_order FROM order_items;
-- (3)
WITH x AS (SELECT department, emp_id, monthly_income, NTILE(20) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY monthly_income DESC) AS bucket FROM employees)
SELECT * FROM x WHERE bucket = 1;
-- (4)
WITH p AS (SELECT pr.category, pr.product_id, SUM(oi.sales) AS sales FROM order_items oi JOIN products pr ON pr.product_id = oi.product_id GROUP BY pr.category, pr.product_id),
     n AS (SELECT *, NTILE(10) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY sales DESC) AS decile FROM p)
SELECT * FROM n WHERE decile = 1;
Interview cornerQuestions you may be asked

Q: RANK vs DENSE_RANK vs ROW_NUMBER? ROW_NUMBER numbers rows uniquely; RANK gives ties the same rank and skips following ranks; DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank without gaps.

Q: Find the second-highest salary in each department. CTE with DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC), filter = 2.

Q: How do you remove duplicate rows keeping one? ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY business_key ORDER BY …) and delete rows where it is greater than 1.

Q: Window function vs GROUP BY? Windows keep detail rows and add group-level values; GROUP BY returns one row per group.

SQL for Data Analysis · Lesson 12

Window Functions II: Running Totals, LEAD, LAG & Frames

Build time-series analytics in SQL. Use window frames (ROWS BETWEEN) for running totals and moving averages, LAG and LEAD for month-on-month and year-on-year growth, FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE, cumulative percentages, PERCENT_RANK, CUME_DIST and PERCENTILE_CONT, and gaps-and-islands patterns.

● SQL class 5–6✦ SQL Server 2022, 2026Advanced⏱ 130 min
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Define a window frame with ROWS BETWEEN and explain the default frame when ORDER BY is present
  • Calculate running totals, moving averages and cumulative shares
  • Compare each row with the previous or next row using LAG and LEAD (MoM, YoY, gaps)
  • Use FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE and NTH_VALUE, PERCENT_RANK, CUME_DIST and PERCENTILE_CONT
  • Solve streak and gap problems with ROW_NUMBER differences

Window frames

Inside OVER, ORDER BY defines the order and an optional frame defines which rows around the current row the function uses.

SQL
SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY p ORDER BY d
             ROWS BETWEEN <start> AND <end>)
Frame boundary Meaning
UNBOUNDED PRECEDING From the first row of the partition
n PRECEDING n rows before the current row
CURRENT ROW The current row
n FOLLOWING n rows after
UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING To the last row of the partition
Common mistakesThe default frame trap

When ORDER BY is present and no frame is written, SQL Server uses RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. RANGE treats rows with the same ORDER BY value as peers and includes them all, which gives surprising results with ties, and LAST_VALUE then returns the current row's value. For running totals always write ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW explicitly; it is also much faster.

Running totals

First build the monthly sales table, then add a running (cumulative) total and a share:

SQL
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT YEAR(order_date) AS yr, MONTH(order_date) AS mth, SUM(sales) AS sales
    FROM superstore
    GROUP BY YEAR(order_date), MONTH(order_date)
)
SELECT yr, mth,
       ROUND(sales, 0) AS sales,
       ROUND(SUM(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY yr ORDER BY mth
                              ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 0) AS ytd_sales,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY yr ORDER BY mth
                              ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
                   / SUM(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY yr), 1)                          AS ytd_pct_of_year
FROM monthly
ORDER BY yr, mth;
Result
yr mth sales ytd_sales ytd_pct_of_year
2023 1 2,447,151 2,447,151 4.2
2023 2 3,861,852 6,309,002 10.9
2023 3 3,441,306 9,750,308 16.9
2023 4 3,927,557 13,677,865 23.7
2023 5 4,840,130 18,517,994 32.1
2023 6 5,785,712 24,303,706 42.2
2023 7 5,390,409 29,694,115 51.5
2023 8 4,129,386 33,823,500 58.7
2023 9 5,714,731 39,538,231 68.6
2023 10 5,134,331 44,672,561 77.5
2023 11 5,815,308 50,487,869 87.6
2023 12 7,152,348 57,640,217 100.0
2024 1 6,022,738 6,022,738 9.2
2024 2 2,463,147 8,485,885 13.0
36 rows × 5 columns (first 14 shown)

PARTITION BY yr restarts the running total every January (year-to-date). The percentage uses a second window (the whole year) as the denominator.

Moving averages

A moving average smooths noisy data and shows the trend. Here is the 7-day average of daily units sold:

SQL
SELECT date, units_sold,
       ROUND(AVG(units_sold * 1.0) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS avg_7_day
FROM daily_sales
WHERE date >= '2025-11-01'
ORDER BY date;
Result
date units_sold avg_7_day
2025-11-01 387 387.0
2025-11-02 396 391.5
2025-11-03 353 378.7
2025-11-04 348 371.0
2025-11-05 356 368.0
2025-11-06 350 365.0
2025-11-07 358 364.0
2025-11-08 357 359.7
61 rows × 3 columns (first 8 shown)

The first six rows of a 7-row window have fewer than seven rows available: SQL averages whatever exists (partial windows). Check COUNT(*) OVER (...) if you need to exclude them.

LAG and LEAD: compare with previous and next rows

Function Returns
LAG(col, n, default) The value n rows before the current row (default n = 1)
LEAD(col, n, default) The value n rows after
SQL
WITH monthly AS (
    SELECT YEAR(order_date) * 100 + MONTH(order_date) AS ym, SUM(sales) AS sales
    FROM superstore
    GROUP BY YEAR(order_date) * 100 + MONTH(order_date)
)
SELECT ym,
       ROUND(sales, 0)                                               AS sales,
       ROUND(LAG(sales)  OVER (ORDER BY ym), 0)                      AS prev_month,
       ROUND(100.0 * (sales - LAG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY ym)) / LAG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY ym), 1) AS mom_pct,
       ROUND(LAG(sales, 12) OVER (ORDER BY ym), 0)                   AS same_month_last_year,
       ROUND(100.0 * (sales - LAG(sales, 12) OVER (ORDER BY ym)) / LAG(sales, 12) OVER (ORDER BY ym), 1) AS yoy_pct,
       ROUND(LEAD(sales) OVER (ORDER BY ym), 0)                      AS next_month
FROM monthly
ORDER BY ym;
Result
ym sales prev_month mom_pct same_month_last_year yoy_pct next_month
202301 2,447,151 NULL NULL NULL NULL 3,861,852
202302 3,861,852 2,447,151 57.8 NULL NULL 3,441,306
202303 3,441,306 3,861,852 -10.9 NULL NULL 3,927,557
202304 3,927,557 3,441,306 14.1 NULL NULL 4,840,130
202305 4,840,130 3,927,557 23.2 NULL NULL 5,785,712
202306 5,785,712 4,840,130 19.5 NULL NULL 5,390,409
202307 5,390,409 5,785,712 -6.8 NULL NULL 4,129,386
202308 4,129,386 5,390,409 -23.4 NULL NULL 5,714,731
202309 5,714,731 4,129,386 38.4 NULL NULL 5,134,331
202310 5,134,331 5,714,731 -10.2 NULL NULL 5,815,308
202311 5,815,308 5,134,331 13.3 NULL NULL 7,152,348
202312 7,152,348 5,815,308 23.0 NULL NULL 6,022,738
36 rows × 7 columns (first 12 shown)
  • MoM compares with LAG(sales, 1); YoY compares with LAG(sales, 12) when there is exactly one row per month. This is the SQL equivalent of the pivot table's "Difference From" settings (Excel Lesson 8).
  • The first row has no previous value, so LAG returns NULL (or the default you supply: LAG(sales, 1, 0)).
Watch outGaps in the data

LAG(sales, 12) assumes every month exists. If a month has no sales it also has no row, so LAG(12) points at the wrong month. Build a calendar table (a list of every month) and LEFT JOIN the sales onto it first.

Time between events

"How many days passed between each customer's consecutive orders?"

SQL
WITH o AS (
    SELECT customer_id, order_date,
           LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS prev_order
    FROM orders
)
SELECT COUNT(*)                                          AS repeat_orders,
       ROUND(AVG(DATEDIFF(day, prev_order, order_date) * 1.0), 1) AS avg_days_between_orders,
       MIN(DATEDIFF(day, prev_order, order_date))        AS shortest_gap,
       MAX(DATEDIFF(day, prev_order, order_date))        AS longest_gap
FROM o
WHERE prev_order IS NOT NULL;
Result
repeat_orders avg_days_between_orders shortest_gap longest_gap
2415 186.6 0 1001
1 rows × 4 columns

FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE

SQL
SELECT department, emp_id, monthly_income,
       FIRST_VALUE(emp_id) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY monthly_income DESC)               AS top_earner,
       LAST_VALUE(emp_id)  OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY monthly_income DESC
                                 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING)             AS lowest_earner,
       monthly_income - FIRST_VALUE(monthly_income) OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY monthly_income DESC) AS gap_to_top
FROM employees
ORDER BY department, monthly_income DESC;
Result
department emp_id monthly_income top_earner lowest_earner gap_to_top
Finance E00519 209833 E00519 E00322 0
Finance E00145 185500 E00519 E00322 -24333
Finance E00336 174417 E00519 E00322 -35416
Finance E00201 169500 E00519 E00322 -40333
Finance E01172 168167 E00519 E00322 -41666
Finance E01151 155167 E00519 E00322 -54666
Finance E00759 152083 E00519 E00322 -57750
Finance E01004 144667 E00519 E00322 -65166
1,500 rows × 6 columns (first 8 shown)

LAST_VALUE needs the explicit full frame (UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING); with the default frame it just returns the current row.

Distribution functions

Function Meaning
PERCENT_RANK() (rank − 1) ÷ (rows − 1): 0 for the lowest, 1 for the highest
CUME_DIST() Share of rows with a value ≤ the current one
PERCENTILE_CONT(p) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x) OVER (…) Interpolated percentile (e.g. median at p = 0.5)
PERCENTILE_DISC(p) … An actual value from the data
SQL
SELECT DISTINCT department,
       ROUND(PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY monthly_income) OVER (PARTITION BY department), 0) AS median_income,
       ROUND(AVG(monthly_income) OVER (PARTITION BY department), 0)                                          AS mean_income
FROM employees
ORDER BY department;
Result
department median_income mean_income
Finance 77,709 83,681
HR 86,833 87,805
IT 68,750 79,051
Operations 92,667 92,461
R&D 70,250 80,255
Sales 74,709 82,448
6 rows × 3 columns

In SQL Server, PERCENTILE_CONT is a window function (needs OVER); PostgreSQL uses it as an aggregate (GROUP BY). Mean above median is the signature of a right-skewed distribution (Statistics, ML track).

Cumulative share: the Pareto in SQL

Which products produce the first 80% of sales?

SQL
WITH p AS (
    SELECT product_id, SUM(sales) AS sales FROM order_items GROUP BY product_id
), c AS (
    SELECT product_id, sales,
           SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY sales DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) * 1.0 / SUM(sales) OVER () AS cum_share,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY sales DESC) AS rnk
    FROM p
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS products_for_80pct_of_sales,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM p)  AS total_products
FROM c
WHERE cum_share <= 0.8;
Result
products_for_80pct_of_sales total_products
20 78
1 rows × 2 columns

Gaps and islands: streaks

A classic: find runs of consecutive days. The trick is that date − ROW_NUMBER() is constant within a streak.

SQL
WITH days AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT order_date AS d FROM orders WHERE order_date >= '2025-12-01'
), g AS (
    SELECT d, DATEADD(day, -ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY d), d) AS grp FROM days
)
SELECT MIN(d) AS streak_start, MAX(d) AS streak_end, COUNT(*) AS days_in_streak
FROM g
GROUP BY grp
ORDER BY streak_start;
Result
streak_start streak_end days_in_streak
2025-12-01 2025-12-31 31
1 rows × 3 columns

Each group of consecutive order days becomes one row: all of December 2025 had orders every day, so there is a single streak. The same pattern finds consecutive login days, uninterrupted employment spells and missing-sequence ranges.

Summary

Key takeaways
  • Frames (ROWS BETWEEN … AND …) choose the rows around the current row; always write ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for running totals (the default RANGE frame includes ties).
  • Running totals, YTD, cumulative % and moving averages use aggregate functions with frames.
  • LAG/LEAD read the previous/next row (MoM, YoY, time between events); fill calendar gaps first.
  • FIRST_VALUE/LAST_VALUE need an explicit full frame for LAST_VALUE.
  • PERCENT_RANK, CUME_DIST, PERCENTILE_CONT describe position and median within a distribution.
  • Gaps and islands: value − ROW_NUMBER() is constant within a consecutive run.
Quick quiz6 questions · tap an answer to check it

1. Which frame gives a 3-month moving average (current and two previous rows)?

Answer: B. Two preceding rows plus the current row make three rows.

2. What does LAG(sales, 12) OVER (ORDER BY ym) return for monthly data?

Answer: B. LAG reads n rows back; with one row per month that is 12 months earlier.

3. Why does LAST_VALUE often return the current row's value?

Answer: A. Specify ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.

4. How do you restart a running total every year?

Answer: B. Each partition has its own running total.

5. In the gaps-and-islands trick, what stays constant inside a streak of consecutive dates?

Answer: C. Both increase by 1 per row, so their difference is constant.

6. Mean income is much higher than median income. What does that suggest?

Answer: B. A long right tail pulls the mean above the median.
ExerciseTime-series practice

(1) Monthly sales per region with MoM %; (2) for each customer, the days since their previous order and a flag for "returned within 30 days"; (3) a 3-month moving average of sales by category; (4) the month when cumulative 2025 sales first exceeded ₹5 crore.

Show solution
SQL
-- (1)
WITH m AS (SELECT region, YEAR(order_date)*100+MONTH(order_date) AS ym, SUM(sales) AS sales FROM superstore GROUP BY region, YEAR(order_date)*100+MONTH(order_date))
SELECT region, ym, ROUND(sales,0) AS sales,
       ROUND(100.0*(sales - LAG(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY ym)) / LAG(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY ym), 1) AS mom_pct FROM m ORDER BY region, ym;
-- (2)
WITH o AS (SELECT customer_id, order_date, LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) AS prev FROM orders)
SELECT customer_id, order_date, DATEDIFF(day, prev, order_date) AS days_since_prev,
       CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(day, prev, order_date) <= 30 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS within_30_days FROM o WHERE prev IS NOT NULL;
-- (3)
WITH m AS (SELECT category, YEAR(order_date)*100+MONTH(order_date) AS ym, SUM(sales) AS sales FROM superstore GROUP BY category, YEAR(order_date)*100+MONTH(order_date))
SELECT category, ym, AVG(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY ym ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma3 FROM m;
-- (4)
WITH m AS (SELECT MONTH(order_date) AS mth, SUM(sales) AS sales FROM superstore WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2025 GROUP BY MONTH(order_date)),
     c AS (SELECT mth, SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY mth ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS cum FROM m)
SELECT TOP 1 mth FROM c WHERE cum > 50000000 ORDER BY mth;
Interview cornerQuestions you may be asked

Q: How do you calculate a running total in SQL? SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), optionally partitioned.

Q: How do you calculate month-on-month growth? Aggregate to months, then (sales − LAG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY month)) / LAG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY month); use LAG(…, 12) for YoY.

Q: ROWS vs RANGE in a window frame? ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE includes all rows with the same ORDER BY value as the current row (peers). ROWS is predictable and faster.

Q: How would you find consecutive login days? Gaps and islands: date − ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user ORDER BY date) as a group key, then GROUP BY it.

SQL for Data Analysis · Lesson 13

CTEs, Views, Temporary Tables, Stored Procedures & Functions

Write queries other people can read and reuse. Use CTEs (including recursive CTEs for hierarchies and calendars), create views for reusable logic and security, use temp tables and table variables, and build stored procedures, user-defined functions, parameters and basic error handling in T-SQL.

● SQL class 6✦ SQL Server 2022, 2026Advanced⏱ 130 min
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Structure complex queries with one or more CTEs and explain CTE vs subquery vs temp table
  • Write recursive CTEs for hierarchies (org charts) and number or date series
  • Create, alter and use views, and explain what views are good for
  • Choose between temp tables, table variables and CTEs
  • Write stored procedures with parameters, scalar and table-valued functions, and TRY…CATCH

CTE: a named, readable subquery

A Common Table Expression is a named result set defined with WITH that exists for one statement. It makes complex logic read top to bottom, like paragraphs, instead of inside-out.

SQL
WITH name1 AS (
    SELECT …
),
name2 AS (
    SELECT … FROM name1 …          -- later CTEs can use earlier ones
)
SELECT … FROM name2 …;

From nested subqueries to CTEs

Question: "Which regions had above-average 2025 sales per customer?"

SQL
WITH customer_sales AS (                       -- step 1: sales per customer in 2025
    SELECT c.region, c.customer_id, SUM(oi.sales) AS sales
    FROM order_items AS oi
    JOIN orders    AS o ON o.order_id    = oi.order_id
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND o.order_date < '2026-01-01'
    GROUP BY c.region, c.customer_id
),
region_avg AS (                                -- step 2: average per region
    SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS customers, AVG(sales) AS avg_sales_per_customer
    FROM customer_sales
    GROUP BY region
)
SELECT region, customers,
       ROUND(avg_sales_per_customer, 0)                       AS avg_sales_per_customer,
       ROUND((SELECT AVG(sales) FROM customer_sales), 0)       AS overall_avg
FROM region_avg
WHERE avg_sales_per_customer > (SELECT AVG(sales) FROM customer_sales)   -- step 3: compare
ORDER BY avg_sales_per_customer DESC;
Result
region customers avg_sales_per_customer overall_avg
West 156 142,513 125,805
South 160 130,010 125,805
2 rows × 4 columns

customer_sales is used twice, which with plain subqueries would mean copy-pasting the same block. CTEs also make window-function filters (Lesson 11) clean.

TipCTE style

Name CTEs for what they contain (customer_sales, not cte1); keep each CTE doing one job; comment each step. If a CTE needs a long explanation, it probably should be two CTEs.

CTE, subquery, view and temp table

Subquery / derived table CTE View Temp table
Lives for The statement The statement Permanently (a saved query) The session (#t)
Stores data? No No (re-evaluated) No (unless indexed/materialised) Yes
Reusable in other queries No No Yes In the same session
Can be referenced several times Only by repeating Yes, in the same statement Yes Yes
Recursive No Yes No No
Can be indexed No No Indexed views only Yes
Best for Simple one-off logic Readability, multi-step logic, recursion Sharing logic, hiding complexity, security Large intermediate results used many times
NoteA CTE is not a cache

In SQL Server the CTE's query may run each time it is referenced. If an expensive CTE is used many times, load it into a temp table once.

Recursive CTEs

A recursive CTE has an anchor (starting rows) and a recursive member that refers to the CTE itself, joined with UNION ALL. It repeats until no new rows are produced.

Number and date series

SQL
WITH numbers AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n                      -- anchor
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 7      -- recursive member with a stop condition
)
SELECT n FROM numbers;
Result
n
1
2
3
4
5
6
7
7 rows × 1 columns

A calendar table of every day in 2026, handy for filling gaps before LAG/LEAD (Lesson 12):

SQL
WITH calendar AS (
    SELECT CAST('2026-01-01' AS DATE) AS d
    UNION ALL
    SELECT CAST(DATEADD(day, 1, d) AS DATE) FROM calendar WHERE d < CAST('2026-12-31' AS DATE)
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS days, MIN(d) AS first_day, MAX(d) AS last_day,
       SUM(CASE WHEN DATENAME(weekday, d) IN ('Saturday', 'Sunday') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS weekend_days
FROM calendar;
Result
days first_day last_day weekend_days
365 2026-01-01 2026-12-31 104
1 rows × 4 columns

In SQL Server, the default limit is 100 recursions, so a year-long calendar needs OPTION (MAXRECURSION 400) after the final SELECT (use 0 for no limit, with care).

Hierarchies: org chart

SQL
CREATE TABLE org (emp_id INT, name VARCHAR(20), manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO org VALUES (1,'Varun',NULL), (2,'Asha',1), (3,'Ravi',1), (4,'Meera',2), (5,'Kabir',2), (6,'Zoya',4), (7,'Farhan',3);

WITH tree AS (
    SELECT emp_id, name, manager_id, 0 AS level, CAST(name AS VARCHAR(200)) AS path
    FROM org WHERE manager_id IS NULL                              -- anchor: the top
    UNION ALL
    SELECT o.emp_id, o.name, o.manager_id, t.level + 1, CAST(CONCAT(t.path, ' > ', o.name) AS VARCHAR(200))
    FROM org AS o
    JOIN tree AS t ON o.manager_id = t.emp_id                      -- walk down one level
)
SELECT level, CONCAT(REPLICATE('    ', level), name) AS org_chart, path
FROM tree
ORDER BY path;
Result
Commands completed successfully.
(7 rows affected)
level org_chart path
0 Varun Varun
1 Asha Varun > Asha
2 Kabir Varun > Asha > Kabir
2 Meera Varun > Asha > Meera
3 Zoya Varun > Asha > Meera > Zoya
1 Ravi Varun > Ravi
2 Farhan Varun > Ravi > Farhan
7 rows × 3 columns

Recursive CTEs also solve bill-of-materials, category trees and graph-path problems.

Views

A view is a saved SELECT with a name. Querying it runs the stored query; it holds no data of its own.

SQL
CREATE VIEW vw_order_detail AS
SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date, o.ship_mode,
       c.customer_id, c.customer_name, c.segment, c.city, c.region,
       p.product_id, p.product_name, p.category, p.sub_category,
       oi.quantity, oi.discount, oi.sales, oi.profit
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN orders    AS o ON o.order_id    = oi.order_id
JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
JOIN products  AS p ON p.product_id  = oi.product_id;

SELECT category, region, ROUND(SUM(sales), 0) AS sales
FROM vw_order_detail
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY category, region
ORDER BY category, region;
Result
category region sales
Furniture East 2,875,816
Furniture North 2,688,426
Furniture South 3,759,688
Furniture West 3,436,316
Office Supplies East 1,075,076
Office Supplies North 833,204
Office Supplies South 1,018,343
Office Supplies West 1,044,699
Technology East 14,959,309
Technology North 12,911,446
Technology South 16,023,523
Technology West 17,750,953
12 rows × 3 columns

Now analysts query one friendly object instead of repeating a four-table join. Power BI and Excel can connect to the view too.

Use views to Notes
Hide complexity One name for a multi-join query
Provide one definition of a metric "Net sales" defined once, used everywhere
Secure data GRANT SELECT ON vw_sales_summary TO analysts without granting access to base tables; expose only some columns/rows
Keep apps working when tables change Change the view, not every report

SQL Server syntax: CREATE VIEW dbo.vw_x AS …, ALTER VIEW, DROP VIEW IF EXISTS, CREATE OR ALTER VIEW. Rules: no ORDER BY inside a view (unless with TOP); views can usually be INSERT/UPDATEd only if they map simply to one table. Indexed (materialised) views store the results physically for speed (WITH SCHEMABINDING + a unique clustered index).

Temporary tables and table variables

SQL
-- Temp table: lives for the session, stored in tempdb, can be indexed, has statistics
SELECT customer_id, SUM(sales) AS sales
INTO   #cust_sales                      -- the # prefix makes it local temporary
FROM   superstore
GROUP  BY customer_id;

CREATE INDEX ix_cust ON #cust_sales (customer_id);
SELECT TOP 10 * FROM #cust_sales ORDER BY sales DESC;
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS #cust_sales;

-- Table variable: scoped to the batch; for small row counts
DECLARE @top TABLE (customer_id VARCHAR(10), sales DECIMAL(14,2));
INSERT INTO @top SELECT TOP 5 customer_id, SUM(sales) FROM superstore GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY SUM(sales) DESC;
SELECT * FROM @top;

##name is a global temp table visible to other sessions. Temp tables vanish when the session ends.

Stored procedures

A stored procedure is a named, saved block of T-SQL that can take parameters, run many statements, and return results. It is compiled and its plan cached, and permissions can be granted on the procedure instead of the tables.

SQL
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE dbo.usp_sales_by_region
    @from_date DATE,
    @to_date   DATE,
    @category  VARCHAR(30) = NULL          -- optional parameter with a default
AS
BEGIN
    SET NOCOUNT ON;                        -- suppress "(n rows affected)" messages

    SELECT c.region,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS orders,
           SUM(oi.sales)              AS sales,
           SUM(oi.profit)             AS profit
    FROM dbo.order_items AS oi
    JOIN dbo.orders      AS o ON o.order_id    = oi.order_id
    JOIN dbo.customers   AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    JOIN dbo.products    AS p ON p.product_id  = oi.product_id
    WHERE o.order_date >= @from_date
      AND o.order_date <  DATEADD(day, 1, @to_date)
      AND (@category IS NULL OR p.category = @category)     -- optional filter
    GROUP BY c.region
    ORDER BY sales DESC;
END;
GO

EXEC dbo.usp_sales_by_region @from_date = '2025-01-01', @to_date = '2025-12-31';
EXEC dbo.usp_sales_by_region '2025-01-01', '2025-12-31', 'Technology';

Output parameters, variables, IF and loops

SQL
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE dbo.usp_add_order_note
    @order_id VARCHAR(20),
    @note     NVARCHAR(200),
    @rows     INT OUTPUT
AS
BEGIN
    SET NOCOUNT ON;
    IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dbo.orders WHERE order_id = @order_id)
    BEGIN
        RAISERROR('Order %s does not exist.', 16, 1, @order_id);   -- or THROW 50001, 'Order does not exist.', 1;
        RETURN;
    END;

    UPDATE dbo.orders SET note = @note WHERE order_id = @order_id;
    SET @rows = @@ROWCOUNT;                                         -- rows changed by the last statement
END;
GO

DECLARE @n INT;
EXEC dbo.usp_add_order_note 'IN-2025-00042', N'Gift wrap', @rows = @n OUTPUT;
SELECT @n AS rows_updated;
Control flow Syntax
Condition IF … BEGIN … END ELSE BEGIN … END
Loop WHILE @i <= 10 BEGIN … SET @i += 1; END
Exit / return RETURN
Row count @@ROWCOUNT
Dynamic SQL EXEC sp_executesql @sql, N'@x INT', @x = 5 (use parameters; never concatenate user input: SQL injection)

Error handling: TRY…CATCH

SQL
BEGIN TRY
    BEGIN TRAN;
        UPDATE dbo.accounts SET balance = balance - 5000 WHERE acct_id = 1;
        UPDATE dbo.accounts SET balance = balance + 5000 WHERE acct_id = 2;
    COMMIT;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 ROLLBACK;
    SELECT ERROR_NUMBER() AS err_no, ERROR_MESSAGE() AS err_msg, ERROR_LINE() AS err_line;
    THROW;                                       -- re-raise to the caller
END CATCH;

User-defined functions (UDFs)

Type Returns Example use
Scalar One value dbo.fn_margin(profit, sales)
Inline table-valued A table, from one SELECT dbo.fn_orders_by_city('Pune'): like a parameterised view
Multi-statement table-valued A table built in a body Complex logic (usually slower)
SQL
CREATE OR ALTER FUNCTION dbo.fn_margin (@profit DECIMAL(12,2), @sales DECIMAL(12,2))
RETURNS DECIMAL(6,2)
AS
BEGIN
    RETURN CASE WHEN @sales = 0 THEN NULL ELSE 100.0 * @profit / @sales END;
END;
GO

CREATE OR ALTER FUNCTION dbo.fn_sales_by_city (@city VARCHAR(30))
RETURNS TABLE
AS RETURN (
    SELECT order_id, order_date, sales, profit FROM dbo.vw_order_detail WHERE city = @city
);
GO

SELECT order_id, dbo.fn_margin(profit, sales) AS margin_pct FROM dbo.fn_sales_by_city('Pune');
Watch outScalar UDFs can be slow

Older SQL Server versions call a scalar UDF once per row, which can make a query many times slower than writing the expression inline (SQL Server 2019+ can inline some). Prefer inline table-valued functions or views for set-based logic.

Procedure vs function vs view

View Stored procedure Function
Parameters No Yes Yes
Can change data (INSERT/UPDATE) Limited Yes No (side-effect free)
Used in SELECT / FROM Yes No (EXEC) Yes
Returns A table Result sets, output parameters, a status code A value or a table

Triggers (awareness)

A trigger runs automatically on INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE: audit logs, maintaining summary tables. Use sparingly: they hide logic and can slow writes. Modern designs prefer explicit procedures, constraints, temporal tables or change data capture.

Do it with AIDo it with AI

Prompt: "Convert this nested-subquery SQL into readable CTEs with clear names and comments, keep the result identical, and explain each step." AI is good at refactoring; verify equality by running both versions and comparing with EXCEPT in both directions (Lesson 9).

Summary

Key takeaways
  • CTE (WITH name AS (…)): a named, readable subquery for one statement; can be referenced many times; recursive CTEs generate series and walk hierarchies (anchor + UNION ALL + recursive member).
  • View: a saved query for reuse, one definition of a metric, and security. Temp tables (#t) store intermediate data and can be indexed; table variables suit small sets.
  • Stored procedures take parameters, run multiple statements, change data and handle errors with TRY…CATCH; functions return values or tables and can be used inside queries.
  • Prefer set-based SQL; avoid row-by-row loops and scalar UDFs on big tables; never concatenate user input into dynamic SQL.
Quick quiz6 questions · tap an answer to check it

1. A CTE exists for:

Answer: B. A CTE is defined and used within one statement.

2. What are the two parts of a recursive CTE?

Answer: B. The anchor gives starting rows; the recursive member repeats until nothing new appears.

3. Which object stores data physically for the session and can be indexed?

Answer: C.

temp tables live in tempdb for the session.

4. Which can modify data and return an OUTPUT parameter?

Answer: B. Procedures can run INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and return output parameters.

5. Why grant access to a view instead of the base table?

Answer: B. Views are a security and simplification layer.

6. A recursive CTE stops with an error after 100 levels. Fix?

Answer: B. SQL Server's default recursion limit is 100.
ExerciseBuild reusable objects

(1) A view vw_monthly_sales with year, month, category and total sales. (2) A CTE query that lists, for each region, the best-selling sub-category and its share of the region's sales. (3) A stored procedure usp_top_customers (@year INT, @n INT) that returns the top n customers by sales for a year. (4) A recursive CTE that lists all employees under manager 2 in the org table with their level.

Show solution
SQL
-- (1)
CREATE VIEW vw_monthly_sales AS
SELECT YEAR(order_date) AS yr, MONTH(order_date) AS mth, category, SUM(sales) AS sales FROM vw_order_detail GROUP BY YEAR(order_date), MONTH(order_date), category;
-- (2)
WITH rs AS (SELECT region, sub_category, SUM(sales) AS sales FROM superstore GROUP BY region, sub_category),
     r  AS (SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY sales DESC) AS rnk, 100.0*sales/SUM(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY region) AS pct FROM rs)
SELECT region, sub_category, ROUND(pct,1) AS pct_of_region FROM r WHERE rnk = 1;
-- (3) T-SQL
CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE usp_top_customers @year INT, @n INT AS
BEGIN
  SELECT TOP (@n) customer_id, customer_name, SUM(sales) AS sales FROM vw_order_detail WHERE YEAR(order_date) = @year
  GROUP BY customer_id, customer_name ORDER BY sales DESC;
END;
-- (4)
WITH t AS (SELECT emp_id, name, 1 AS level FROM org WHERE manager_id = 2
           UNION ALL SELECT o.emp_id, o.name, t.level + 1 FROM org o JOIN t ON o.manager_id = t.emp_id)
SELECT * FROM t;
Interview cornerQuestions you may be asked

Q: CTE vs temp table vs subquery? Subquery: inline, single use. CTE: named, readable, statement-scoped, supports recursion, may be re-evaluated. Temp table: materialised data for the session, indexable: use for large intermediate results reused many times.

Q: View vs stored procedure? A view is a saved SELECT you query like a table; a procedure is a program with parameters and multiple statements that can change data.

Q: What is a recursive CTE and where do you use it? A CTE that references itself, for hierarchies (org charts, categories), series generation and graph traversal.

Q: How do you prevent SQL injection in dynamic SQL? Use parameterised sp_executesql and QUOTENAME for identifiers; never concatenate raw user input.

SQL for Data Analysis · Lesson 14

Transactions, Indexes, Performance & Security

Make SQL safe and fast. Understand transactions and ACID (BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVE), isolation and locking, indexes (clustered, non-clustered, covering), how to read an execution plan, a checklist for writing fast queries, and permissions with GRANT, REVOKE and roles (DCL).

● SQL class 6 (extended)✦ SQL Server 2022, 2026Advanced⏱ 110 min
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Explain ACID and group statements into transactions that commit or roll back together
  • Describe isolation levels, locks, blocking and deadlocks at an analyst level
  • Choose between clustered and non-clustered indexes and recognise queries that can or cannot use them
  • Read the basics of an execution plan and apply a performance checklist
  • Grant and revoke permissions with roles, and apply least privilege

Transactions and ACID

A transaction is a group of statements treated as one unit of work: all succeed (commit) or none do (rollback). Moving ₹5,000 between two accounts is two updates; if the server crashes between them, money would vanish without a transaction.

Property Meaning Example
Atomicity All or nothing Both account updates happen, or neither
Consistency Data stays valid (constraints hold) Total money before = total after; no negative balance if a CHECK forbids it
Isolation Concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-finished work Another user does not see the debit without the credit
Durability Once committed, it survives a crash Transaction log is written to disk first

Transaction commands

Command Purpose
BEGIN TRANSACTION (BEGIN TRAN) Start a transaction
COMMIT Make all changes permanent
ROLLBACK Undo everything since BEGIN (or since a savepoint)
SAVE TRANSACTION name Create a savepoint inside the transaction
ROLLBACK TRANSACTION name Undo back to the savepoint only
@@TRANCOUNT How many transactions are open (should be 0 when you leave)

By default SQL Server runs in autocommit mode: every single statement is its own transaction. Wrap several statements in BEGIN TRAN … COMMIT to group them.

Seeing a rollback

SQL
CREATE TABLE accounts (acct_id INT PRIMARY KEY, holder VARCHAR(20), balance DECIMAL(12,2));
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 'Asha', 20000), (2, 'Ravi', 5000);

BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 5000 WHERE acct_id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 5000 WHERE acct_id = 2;
SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY acct_id;      -- inside the transaction: changes visible to us
ROLLBACK;                                     -- something went wrong: undo both updates

SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY acct_id;      -- balances are back to the originals
Result
Commands completed successfully.
(2 rows affected)
Commands completed successfully.
(1 row affected)
(1 row affected)
Commands completed successfully.
Result set 1
acct_id holder balance
1 Asha 15,000
2 Ravi 10,000
2 rows × 3 columns
Result set 2
acct_id holder balance
1 Asha 20,000
2 Ravi 5,000
2 rows × 3 columns

The safe-update pattern

The pattern that protects you from the "UPDATE without WHERE" disaster (Lesson 4):

SQL
BEGIN TRAN;

UPDATE dbo.staff SET salary = salary * 1.05 WHERE dept_id = 10;

SELECT @@ROWCOUNT AS rows_changed;                    -- expected: 2?
SELECT emp_id, salary FROM dbo.staff WHERE dept_id = 10;     -- sanity-check

-- If everything looks right:
COMMIT;
-- Otherwise:
-- ROLLBACK;
Watch outNever leave a transaction open

An open transaction holds locks that block other users and keeps the log from truncating. Always end with COMMIT or ROLLBACK; check SELECT @@TRANCOUNT; if a query window seems "stuck".

Concurrency: isolation, locks and deadlocks

When many users work at once, the database uses locks to keep transactions isolated. Isolation levels trade consistency for concurrency:

Level Prevents Notes
READ UNCOMMITTED Nothing (allows dirty reads; NOLOCK hint) Can read data that is later rolled back; avoid for reports needing accuracy
READ COMMITTED (default) Dirty reads A row you read can change before you read it again
REPEATABLE READ Dirty and non-repeatable reads Holds read locks longer
SERIALIZABLE Also phantom rows Safest, least concurrent
SNAPSHOT / RCSI Readers do not block writers (row versions) Common in modern systems, uses tempdb
  • Blocking: one session waits for a lock held by another. Fix: shorter transactions, indexes, row versioning.
  • Deadlock: two sessions each hold a lock the other needs; SQL Server kills one (the "victim", error 1205). Fix: access tables in the same order, keep transactions short, retry on error 1205.

Indexes: how databases find rows fast

Without an index, a query like WHERE customer_id = 'C0042' scans every row (table scan). An index is a sorted structure (a B-tree) that lets the database jump straight to matching rows, like the index of a book.

Index type What it is How many per table
Clustered Defines the physical order of the table's rows; the table is the index. Created by default with a PRIMARY KEY One
Non-clustered A separate sorted copy of selected columns with pointers to the rows Many (up to 999)
Unique Enforces uniqueness (created for UNIQUE constraints) Many
Covering (INCLUDE) A non-clustered index that contains every column a query needs, so the table is never touched
Filtered Indexes only rows matching a condition
Columnstore Column-wise compressed storage for analytics on huge tables
SQL
CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX cx_orders_date ON dbo.orders (order_date);           -- if not already clustered by the PK

CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX ix_orders_customer
    ON dbo.orders (customer_id)
    INCLUDE (order_date, ship_mode);                                          -- covering index for "orders per customer" queries

CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX ix_items_product ON dbo.order_items (product_id);   -- foreign keys deserve indexes

DROP INDEX ix_orders_customer ON dbo.orders;
SQL
CREATE INDEX ix_super_city ON superstore (city);
SELECT index_name, table_name FROM duckdb_indexes() WHERE table_name = 'superstore';
Result
index_name table_name
ix_super_city superstore
1 rows × 2 columns

Which queries can use an index?

Pattern Uses an index? Why
WHERE customer_id = 'C0042' Yes (seek) Equality on the leading column
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND order_date < '2026-01-01' Yes Range on an indexed column
WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2025 No (scan) The function must run on every row: non-SARGable
WHERE customer_name LIKE 'Ra%' Yes Prefix match
WHERE customer_name LIKE '%Rao' No Leading wildcard
WHERE UPPER(city) = 'PUNE' No Function on the column (the default collation is already case-insensitive)
WHERE city = 'Pune' OR product_id = 'P0012' Often no OR across different columns
WHERE CAST(order_id AS VARCHAR) = '1001' No Type conversion on the column
TipSARGable predicates

SARG = Search ARGument able. Keep the column bare on one side of the comparison and do the maths on the other side: use order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND order_date < '2026-01-01' instead of YEAR(order_date) = 2025, and sales > 100 / 1.18 instead of sales * 1.18 > 100.

Index trade-offs

Indexes speed up reads but slow down writes (every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also update each index) and use disk space. Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY and GROUP BY, and foreign keys; do not index everything. Analytic warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery) use different techniques (partitioning, clustering, columnar storage) instead of manual indexes.

Execution plans

In SSMS press Ctrl + L (estimated plan) or Ctrl + M then run (actual plan). The plan is a diagram of operators read right to left. Things to look for:

Operator Meaning Concern
Index Seek Direct lookup Good
Index / Clustered Index Scan Reads many rows Fine for big reports, suspicious for single-row lookups
Table Scan Reads the heap Usually add an index
Key Lookup Fetches extra columns from the table per row Consider a covering index (INCLUDE)
Hash / Merge / Nested Loops Join Join algorithms Hash for big unsorted inputs; nested loops for small; merge for sorted
Sort Sorting rows Expensive; an index in the right order avoids it
Thick arrows, big estimated vs actual row differences Bad estimates Update statistics

SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON; shows logical reads (the best measure of work) and CPU time for each query.

Performance checklist for analysts

  1. Select only the columns and rows you need: avoid SELECT *; filter early.
  2. Make filters SARGable (no functions on columns; use ranges for dates).
  3. Join on indexed keys with matching data types (an INT joined to a VARCHAR forces conversions).
  4. Aggregate before joining when joining big tables (reduce rows first, avoids row explosion).
  5. UNION ALL instead of UNION; EXISTS instead of IN (huge list); avoid DISTINCT as a bandage for join duplicates.
  6. Avoid row-by-row logic (cursors, scalar UDF in WHERE); think in sets.
  7. Test on realistic data; look at the actual plan; keep statistics updated.
  8. Pull less data into BI tools: summarise in SQL, or create views and aggregate tables.
  9. Limit while developing: SELECT TOP 100 or WHERE on a date range, then remove it.

Security: DCL

Data Control Language gives and removes permissions. Follow the principle of least privilege: grant only what each person or application needs.

SQL
-- Logins (server level) and users (database level)
CREATE LOGIN priya_analyst WITH PASSWORD = 'Use-A-Strong-Passphrase-1!';
CREATE USER  priya_analyst FOR LOGIN priya_analyst;

-- Roles group permissions
CREATE ROLE analyst_role;
GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA::dbo        TO analyst_role;          -- read all tables in dbo
DENY  SELECT ON dbo.customers (phone, email) TO analyst_role;     -- but hide personal columns
GRANT EXECUTE ON dbo.usp_sales_by_region TO analyst_role;

ALTER ROLE analyst_role ADD MEMBER priya_analyst;            -- SQL Server 2012+: ALTER ROLE … ADD MEMBER

REVOKE SELECT ON dbo.orders FROM analyst_role;                -- take back a permission
Statement Effect
GRANT Gives a permission
REVOKE Removes a previously granted (or denied) permission
DENY Explicitly blocks a permission (overrides grants)
Fixed roles db_datareader (read all), db_datawriter, db_owner (full control: avoid)

Other protections: Row-Level Security (a region manager sees only their rows), Dynamic Data Masking (show XXXX-1234), Always Encrypted and TDE (encryption), auditing, and never embedding passwords in scripts (use Windows/Entra ID authentication or a secret store). In India, personal data handling also falls under the DPDP Act 2023: collect only what you need and restrict who can see it.

Do it with AIDo it with AI

Paste a slow query and its actual execution plan (as XML or text) into an assistant: "Explain what this plan is doing and suggest indexes or rewrites. Do not invent columns." AI can spot scans, key lookups and non-SARGable filters quickly, but test every suggestion; an index that helps one query can hurt a hundred writes.

Summary

Key takeaways
  • A transaction groups statements to commit or roll back together; ACID = atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability. Use BEGIN TRAN … COMMIT/ROLLBACK, check @@ROWCOUNT, never leave transactions open.
  • Isolation levels and locks keep concurrent users consistent; blocking and deadlocks are managed with short transactions and consistent access order.
  • Indexes (clustered = row order, one per table; non-clustered = separate structure; covering = INCLUDE) speed up reads and slow writes. SARGable filters keep the column bare.
  • Read execution plans for scans, key lookups and bad estimates; use SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON.
  • DCL: GRANT, REVOKE, DENY, roles, least privilege; protect personal data.
Quick quiz6 questions · tap an answer to check it

1. Which ACID property says that a committed transaction survives a power failure?

Answer: D. Durability: committed changes are written to the log/disk.

2. Which filter can use an index on order_date?

Answer: B. The column must be bare (SARGable); functions on the column force a scan.

3. How many clustered indexes can a table have?

Answer: B. The clustered index defines the physical order, so there can be only one.

4. You ran BEGIN TRAN; UPDATE …; and closed the window. What is the risk?

Answer: A. Open transactions keep locks until committed or rolled back.

5. What does DENY do?

Answer: B. DENY takes precedence over GRANT.

6. In an execution plan, a "Key Lookup" repeated for many rows suggests:

Answer: B. Key lookups fetch missing columns from the table row by row; covering the query avoids them.
ExerciseMake it faster

This query is slow on 50 million order lines: SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2025 AND UPPER(region) = 'WEST' ORDER BY sales DESC; Rewrite it and suggest an index.

Show solution
SQL
SELECT item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity, sales, profit      -- only the needed columns
FROM dbo.order_items
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01' AND order_date < '2026-01-01'    -- SARGable range instead of YEAR()
  AND region = 'West'                                              -- default collation is case-insensitive; no UPPER needed
ORDER BY sales DESC;

CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX ix_items_date_region
ON dbo.order_items (order_date, region) INCLUDE (order_id, product_id, quantity, sales, profit);

Check the actual plan for a seek, compare logical reads with SET STATISTICS IO ON, and consider whether the extra index slows nightly loads.

Interview cornerQuestions you may be asked

Q: What is ACID? Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data persists).

Q: Clustered vs non-clustered index? A clustered index sorts and stores the table rows in index order (one per table). A non-clustered index is a separate structure with pointers to rows (many per table).

Q: Why is WHERE YEAR(date) = 2025 slow? It applies a function to every row, so the index on date cannot be used (non-SARGable). Use a date range.

Q: How do you find and fix a slow query? Look at the actual execution plan and I/O statistics, find scans/lookups/bad estimates, make predicates SARGable, add or adjust indexes, reduce columns/rows early, and re-test.

SQL for Data Analysis · Lesson 15

End-to-End SQL Case Study & Interview Practice

Put everything together. Work through a complete analysis of the retail business (data quality, KPIs, trends, customer segmentation, retention, product and discount analysis) using joins, CTEs and window functions, then practise 25 classic SQL interview questions with model answers.

● SQL class 5 (end-to-end case study)✦ 2026Advanced⏱ 180 min
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Run a structured SQL analysis: understand the data, check quality, calculate KPIs, find drivers, and recommend actions
  • Combine joins, CTEs, aggregation and window functions in multi-step queries
  • Build customer segments (RFM), cohort and retention views in SQL
  • Answer common SQL interview questions with clear, correct queries
  • Explain results in business language

The business problem

Case studyRetail growth review

You are the data analyst at an Indian retailer selling Furniture, Office Supplies and Technology through four regions. Sales grew from 2023 to 2025, but the CFO suspects profit is not keeping pace. Management wants answers to five questions: (1) Is the data trustworthy? (2) How are sales and profit really trending? (3) Where are we losing money and why? (4) Who are our best customers and are they staying? (5) What should we do next quarter?

Step 1: understand the data

SQL
SELECT 'orders'       AS tbl, COUNT(*) AS n, MIN(order_date) AS first_date, MAX(order_date) AS last_date FROM orders
UNION ALL SELECT 'order_items', COUNT(*), NULL, NULL FROM order_items
UNION ALL SELECT 'customers',   COUNT(*), NULL, NULL FROM customers
UNION ALL SELECT 'products',    COUNT(*), NULL, NULL FROM products;
Result
tbl n first_date last_date
orders 3200 2023-01-01 2025-12-31
order_items 6323 NULL NULL
customers 800 NULL NULL
products 78 NULL NULL
4 rows × 4 columns

Grain: order_items has one row per product line in an order; orders one row per order; customers one row per customer. KPIs like "orders" must use COUNT(DISTINCT order_id), and "average order value" needs order-level totals (Lesson 10).

Step 2: data-quality checks

Always check before analysing. A compact data-quality report:

SQL
SELECT
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_items WHERE sales IS NULL OR profit IS NULL OR quantity IS NULL)       AS null_measures,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_items WHERE sales <= 0 OR quantity <= 0)                               AS non_positive,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_items WHERE discount < 0 OR discount > 1)                              AS bad_discount,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE ship_date < order_date)                                         AS ship_before_order,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_items oi LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL) AS orphan_items,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE c.customer_id IS NULL) AS orders_without_customer,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT item_id) FROM order_items)                                      AS duplicate_item_ids;
Result
null_measures non_positive bad_discount ship_before_order orphan_items orders_without_customer duplicate_item_ids
0 0 0 0 0 0 0
1 rows × 7 columns

All zeros: the data is clean, so the numbers can be trusted. In real projects every non-zero here becomes a ticket to fix or a documented exclusion. Also check business-rule outliers:

SQL
SELECT ROUND(MIN(sales), 0) AS min_sales, ROUND(MAX(sales), 0) AS max_sales,
       ROUND(AVG(sales), 0) AS avg_sales,
       MIN(discount) AS min_discount, MAX(discount) AS max_discount,
       MIN(quantity) AS min_qty, MAX(quantity) AS max_qty
FROM order_items;
Result
min_sales max_sales avg_sales min_discount max_discount min_qty max_qty
42 619,290 31,854 0 0.4 1 7
1 rows × 7 columns

Step 3: KPIs and trends

SQL
WITH yearly AS (
    SELECT YEAR(o.order_date)              AS yr,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)      AS orders,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id)   AS customers,
           SUM(oi.sales)                   AS sales,
           SUM(oi.profit)                  AS profit
    FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    GROUP BY YEAR(o.order_date)
)
SELECT yr, orders, customers,
       ROUND(sales, 0)                                           AS sales,
       ROUND(100.0 * (sales - LAG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY yr)) / LAG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY yr), 1)   AS sales_growth_pct,
       ROUND(profit, 0)                                          AS profit,
       ROUND(100.0 * (profit - LAG(profit) OVER (ORDER BY yr)) / LAG(profit) OVER (ORDER BY yr), 1) AS profit_growth_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * profit / sales, 1)                          AS margin_pct,
       ROUND(sales / orders, 0)                                  AS avg_order_value
FROM yearly
ORDER BY yr;
Result
yr orders customers sales sales_growth_pct profit profit_growth_pct margin_pct avg_order_value
2023 883 540 57,640,217 NULL 4,725,378 NULL 8.2 65,278
2024 1085 590 65,396,556 13.5 6,135,992 29.9 9.4 60,273
2025 1232 623 78,376,797 19.8 7,490,793 22.1 9.6 63,618
3 rows × 9 columns

Finding 1. Sales grew 13.5% in 2024 and 19.8% in 2025, and profit grew even faster (29.9% and 22.1%), so the overall margin edged up from 8.2% to 9.6%. The growth is real, but a 9.6% margin is low compared with the 17–18% earned on lines sold without a discount (you will see this in Step 4). The CFO's concern is about the quality of profit: let's look at where the money is made and lost.

Step 4: where do we lose money?

SQL
SELECT p.category, p.sub_category,
       COUNT(*)                                            AS lines,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.sales), 0)                             AS sales,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.profit), 0)                            AS profit,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(oi.profit) / SUM(oi.sales), 1)    AS margin_pct,
       ROUND(AVG(oi.discount) * 100, 1)                    AS avg_discount_pct
FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY p.category, p.sub_category
ORDER BY profit;
Result
category sub_category lines sales profit margin_pct avg_discount_pct
Furniture Tables 505 14,046,224 -816,042 -5.8 17.5
Furniture Bookcases 477 11,274,849 -422,786 -3.7 18.3
Office Supplies Art 462 245,985 36,526 14.8 7.6
Office Supplies Binders 494 401,219 61,074 15.2 7.4
Office Supplies Paper 559 493,232 75,040 15.2 7.2
Furniture Furnishings 442 1,429,307 78,632 5.5 7.4
Furniture Chairs 493 8,091,474 342,043 4.2 8.3
Technology Accessories 445 3,178,930 369,554 11.6 7.5
Office Supplies Storage 507 2,659,340 397,228 14.9 7.6
Office Supplies Appliances 492 6,333,529 944,927 14.9 7.5
Technology Phones 488 31,919,223 3,663,117 11.5 7.1
Technology Machines 491 42,590,335 5,186,711 12.2 6.7
13 rows × 7 columns (first 12 shown)

Finding 2. Tables and Bookcases lose money, and they also carry the heaviest average discounts. Is discounting the cause? Compare margin by discount level and by whether the line is Furniture:

SQL
SELECT CASE WHEN p.category = 'Furniture' THEN 'Furniture' ELSE 'Other' END AS group_name,
       CASE WHEN oi.discount = 0 THEN '0%' WHEN oi.discount <= 0.2 THEN '1–20%' ELSE '>20%' END AS discount_band,
       COUNT(*)                                          AS lines,
       ROUND(SUM(oi.profit), 0)                          AS profit,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(oi.profit) / SUM(oi.sales), 1)  AS margin_pct
FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY CASE WHEN p.category = 'Furniture' THEN 'Furniture' ELSE 'Other' END,
         CASE WHEN oi.discount = 0 THEN '0%' WHEN oi.discount <= 0.2 THEN '1–20%' ELSE '>20%' END
ORDER BY group_name, discount_band;
Result
group_name discount_band lines profit margin_pct
Furniture 0% 850 1,861,761 11.7
Furniture 1–20% 509 -317,393 -3.9
Furniture >20% 558 -2,362,521 -21.9
Other 0% 2630 19,857,203 18.4
Other 1–20% 1434 1,014,534 2.0
Other >20% 342 -1,701,419 -18.9
6 rows × 5 columns

Finding 3. In every group, discounts above 20% destroy margin. Furniture is hit hardest because it is discounted more often. What would profit be if lines discounted above 20% had been sold at a 20% discount instead? A rough "what-if":

SQL
WITH x AS (
    SELECT oi.sales, oi.profit, oi.discount,
           oi.sales / (1 - oi.discount)            AS list_value,
           (oi.sales / (1 - oi.discount)) * 0.8    AS sales_at_20,
           oi.sales - oi.profit                    AS cost
    FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.discount > 0.2
)
SELECT COUNT(*)                                  AS lines_over_20pct,
       ROUND(SUM(profit), 0)                     AS actual_profit,
       ROUND(SUM(sales_at_20 - cost), 0)         AS profit_if_capped_at_20pct,
       ROUND(SUM(sales_at_20 - cost) - SUM(profit), 0) AS potential_gain
FROM x;
Result
lines_over_20pct actual_profit profit_if_capped_at_20pct potential_gain
900 -4,063,940 -422,474 3,641,466
1 rows × 4 columns

(This ignores that a lower discount might lose some of those sales. It is an upper bound to size the opportunity, and it must be labelled as such for management.)

Step 5: customers

Top customers and concentration

SQL
WITH c AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(oi.sales) AS sales, SUM(oi.profit) AS profit, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS orders
    FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    GROUP BY o.customer_id
), r AS (
    SELECT *, NTILE(10) OVER (ORDER BY sales DESC) AS decile FROM c
)
SELECT decile,
       COUNT(*)                                      AS customers,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(sales) / SUM(SUM(sales)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_sales,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(profit) / SUM(SUM(profit)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_profit
FROM r
GROUP BY decile
ORDER BY decile;

decile customers pct_of_sales pct_of_profit

RFM segmentation

RFM scores each customer by Recency (days since last order), Frequency (number of orders) and Monetary value (total sales). The reference date is the day after the last order in the data.

SQL
WITH base AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id,
           DATEDIFF(day, MAX(o.order_date), '2026-01-01')  AS recency_days,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)                      AS frequency,
           SUM(oi.sales)                                   AS monetary
    FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    GROUP BY o.customer_id
), scored AS (
    SELECT *,
           NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY recency_days DESC) AS r,        -- 4 = most recent
           NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY frequency)         AS f,
           NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY monetary)          AS m
    FROM base
)
SELECT customer_id, recency_days, frequency, ROUND(monetary, 0) AS monetary, r, f, m,
       CASE WHEN r >= 3 AND f >= 3 AND m >= 3 THEN 'Champions'
            WHEN r >= 3 AND f >= 2             THEN 'Loyal'
            WHEN r <= 2 AND f >= 3 AND m >= 3  THEN 'At risk (high value)'
            WHEN r = 1                         THEN 'Lost / hibernating'
            ELSE 'Potential' END AS segment
FROM scored
ORDER BY monetary DESC;
Result
customer_id recency_days frequency monetary r f m segment
C0741 441 6 1,204,439 1 4 4 At risk (high value)
C0092 11 8 1,140,540 4 4 4 Champions
C0306 278 7 1,126,867 2 4 4 At risk (high value)
C0781 130 5 1,123,527 2 3 4 At risk (high value)
C0443 92 7 1,113,058 3 4 4 Champions
C0720 12 6 1,100,213 4 4 4 Champions
C0493 514 6 1,004,382 1 4 4 At risk (high value)
C0028 266 5 1,000,189 2 3 4 At risk (high value)
C0630 331 5 1,000,175 1 4 4 At risk (high value)
C0262 70 6 952,738 3 4 4 Champions
785 rows × 8 columns (first 10 shown)
SQL
WITH base AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, DATEDIFF(day, MAX(o.order_date), '2026-01-01') AS recency_days,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS frequency, SUM(oi.sales) AS monetary
    FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY o.customer_id
), scored AS (
    SELECT *, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY recency_days DESC) AS r, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY frequency) AS f, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY monetary) AS m FROM base
), seg AS (
    SELECT *, CASE WHEN r >= 3 AND f >= 3 AND m >= 3 THEN 'Champions' WHEN r >= 3 AND f >= 2 THEN 'Loyal'
                   WHEN r <= 2 AND f >= 3 AND m >= 3 THEN 'At risk (high value)' WHEN r = 1 THEN 'Lost / hibernating' ELSE 'Potential' END AS segment FROM scored
)
SELECT segment, COUNT(*) AS customers, ROUND(SUM(monetary), 0) AS sales,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(monetary) / SUM(SUM(monetary)) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_sales
FROM seg GROUP BY segment ORDER BY sales DESC;
Result
segment customers sales pct_of_sales
Champions 179 80,891,146 40.2
At risk (high value) 93 43,097,520 21.4
Potential 197 29,262,095 14.5
Lost / hibernating 168 24,655,947 12.2
Loyal 148 23,506,862 11.7
5 rows × 4 columns

The "At risk (high value)" group is the first win: high-spending customers who have gone quiet deserve a personal outreach before they churn. The same RFM idea is implemented with pandas in the ML track.

Retention and cohorts

A cohort groups customers by the year of their first order. Retention shows how many come back in later years.

SQL
WITH first_order AS (
    SELECT customer_id, YEAR(MIN(order_date)) AS cohort_year FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
), activity AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, YEAR(order_date) AS active_year FROM orders
)
SELECT f.cohort_year,
       COUNT(DISTINCT f.customer_id)                                            AS cohort_size,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.active_year = f.cohort_year     THEN a.customer_id END) AS y0,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.active_year = f.cohort_year + 1 THEN a.customer_id END) AS y1,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN a.active_year = f.cohort_year + 2 THEN a.customer_id END) AS y2
FROM first_order f
JOIN activity a ON a.customer_id = f.customer_id
GROUP BY f.cohort_year
ORDER BY f.cohort_year;
Result
cohort_year cohort_size y0 y1 y2
2023 540 540 397 415
2024 193 193 156 0
2025 52 52 0 0
3 rows × 5 columns

Divide y1 by cohort_size to get year-1 retention. About 74% of the 2023 cohort (397 of 540) ordered again in 2024, and some who skipped a year returned in 2025: this is a business with sticky customers, so reducing discounts is likely safer than the CFO fears.

Step 6: recommendations

Key takeawaysFindings and actions
  1. Sales and profit are growing, but the margin is only 9.6%, far below the 17–18% earned on undiscounted lines.
  2. Technology produces nearly all the profit; Furniture is net loss-making because Tables and Bookcases are sold with heavy discounts.
  3. Discounts above 20% lose money in every category. Cap discounts at 20% (the what-if sizes the upper-bound upside at about ₹36 lakh over three years; the real gain will be lower if some customers buy less), test in two regions with an A/B design.
  4. Customer base is sticky (strong year-on-year retention), so price discipline is lower-risk than assumed.
  5. Re-engage "At risk (high value)" customers with a targeted offer instead of blanket discounts.
  6. Build a monthly SQL view/dashboard with these KPIs, with data-quality checks as a first step.

Summary

Key takeaways
  • A good analysis follows a workflow: understand the grain, check data quality, calculate KPIs, find drivers, study customers, recommend actions.
  • Always check data quality first; label what-if estimates as estimates.
  • Combine CTEs, joins and window functions to build RFM segments, concentration (Pareto), cohorts and retention.
  • In interviews, state your assumptions, clarify the grain, write clean, formatted SQL, and explain the result in business language.
Quick quiz6 questions · tap an answer to check it

1. Why must "number of orders" use COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) when joining orders to order_items?

Answer: B. The join repeats the order for each of its items.

2. In RFM, a customer with recency 400 days, frequency 1 and low monetary value is probably:

Answer: B. Long time since the last order, few orders and low spend.

3. A cohort table shows 2023 cohort size 500, year-1 active 350. Year-1 retention is:

Answer: B. 350 ÷ 500 = 70%.

4. Which should you do before reporting KPIs?

Answer: B. Untrusted data produces untrusted numbers.

5. The what-if "profit if discounts were capped at 20%" is best described as:

Answer: C. It assumes demand would not change, so it overstates the benefit.

6. NTILE(10) over customers ordered by sales gives:

Answer: B. NTILE splits rows into n buckets.
ExerciseCapstone: your own analysis

Using only SQL on the retail database, prepare a one-page analysis answering: (1) Which three cities have the highest profit and which three the lowest? (2) What is the average days to ship by ship mode, and does a slower mode save money (profit per line)? (3) Which product's sales fell the most from 2024 to 2025? (4) Propose two actions with the numbers that support them.

Show solution

Hints: (1) GROUP BY city with ORDER BY profit ascending and descending using TOP 3 in two queries or RANK() in a CTE. (2) Join orders to order_items, AVG(DATEDIFF(day, order_date, ship_date)) and SUM(profit)/COUNT(*) by ship_mode. (3) Pivot product sales by year with conditional aggregation and compute the difference. (4) Example actions: cap Furniture discounts at 20% in two pilot regions; re-engage at-risk high-value customers. Present each action with a baseline number, an expected impact (labelled as an estimate) and a way to measure success.

Power BI · Lesson 1

Getting Started with Power BI & Your First HR Report

Understand what Power BI is and how its parts fit together, install Power BI Desktop, tour the three views, follow the ETL and analytics stages, and build a complete first report on HR data: cards, bar and column charts, a donut, slicers, a year column with DAX, groups and small multiples.

● Power BI class 1✦ Power BI Desktop 2026 (Copilot, Fabric, PBIP)Beginner⏱ 120 min
By the end of this lesson you can
  • Describe Power BI Desktop, the Service and Mobile, and how data flows between them

What is Power BI?

Power BI is Microsoft's business-intelligence platform: it connects to data, cleans and models it, and turns it into interactive reports and dashboards that people can share. In 2026 it is part of Microsoft Fabric, Microsoft's all-in-one analytics platform, and it is one of the most requested tools in analyst job posts, alongside Excel, SQL and Tableau.

Component What it is Who uses it
Power BI Desktop Free Windows application to build data models and reports (.pbix) Analysts, developers
Power BI Service (app.powerbi.com) Cloud site to publish, share, schedule refresh, create dashboards and apps Analysts and report consumers
Power BI Mobile iOS/Android apps to view reports and get alerts Managers on the go
Power BI Report Builder Paginated, print-ready reports (invoices, statements) Report developers
On-premises data gateway Secure bridge so the cloud can refresh data from your own servers Admins
Power BI Report Server Self-hosted option for organisations that cannot use the cloud IT
Copilot AI assistant that writes DAX, builds report pages and summarises insights (needs a Fabric/Premium capacity) Everyone
TipReport vs dashboard

In Power BI a report is one or more pages of interactive visuals built on a data model. A dashboard (Service only) is a single page of pinned tiles from different reports. Many teams use reports only, or share them as an app.

Licences in brief

Licence Use
Power BI Desktop Free: build and save locally
Free (Service) Personal use in "My workspace"; cannot share with others
Pro Publish and share with other Pro users (about US$14 per user per month)
Premium Per User / Fabric capacity Larger models, AI features, share with free users

(Prices change; check Microsoft's current pricing page.)

Installing Power BI Desktop

Step by stepInstall
  1. Easiest: open the Microsoft Store, search "Power BI Desktop" and click Install (it updates itself every month).
  2. Or download it from the Microsoft Power BI website → Download → Power BI Desktop.
  3. Requirements: Windows 10/11 (64-bit), 4 GB+ RAM (8 GB+ recommended). There is no Mac version: Mac users can use the Service in a browser, a Windows virtual machine, or Windows 365.
  4. Start the app and sign in with a work or school account (optional for building locally).

The three views

View Icon Use it to
Report bar chart Design the report pages
Table (Data) grid Inspect the data and create calculated columns and measures
Model diagram See and edit relationships between tables
DAX query view { } Run DAX queries and test measures

ETL and the analytics process

ETL = Extract (get data from sources), Transform (clean and reshape it), Load (store it in the model). In Power BI, Extract and Transform are done in Power Query, and Load puts the result into the data model. (You met Power Query in Excel Lesson 12: it is the same engine.)

Always start with the question: "Why are people leaving?" decides which data and visuals you need. The worst Power BI reports are tours of every chart type with no question.
